chapter_title: Introduction to High Availability (HA) Concepts and Red Hat's HA Stack
chapter_summary:
High availability is a cornerstone of robust IT infrastructure, particularly in Red Hat enterprise environments where mission-critical applications demand continuous operation. At its core, HA refers to systems designed to operate continuously without failure for a long time, or to recover quickly from failure. The goal is to minimize downtime, ensuring that services remain accessible to users and applications. When we talk about HA, two key metrics immediately come to mind: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO). RTO defines the maximum tolerable duration of time that a computer system, application, or network can be down after a disaster or disruption. It's the "how quickly can we get back up?" question. RPO, on the other hand, specifies the maximum amount of data that can be lost after a disaster. This is the "how much data can we afford to lose?" question. An architect's job is to design systems that meet stringent RTO and RPO requirements, often balancing cost, complexity, and performance.

Failures can manifest in various forms: hardware failures (disk crashes, power supply unit failures), software failures (application bugs, operating system kernel panics), network failures (router outages, cable cuts), and even environmental failures (power outages, natural disasters). A truly highly available system anticipates and mitigates these diverse failure points. Red Hat's approach to high availability primarily leverages the Red Hat High Availability Add-On, which is built upon the open-source Pacemaker and Corosync projects. These tools provide a powerful and flexible framework for creating robust HA clusters on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL). Corosync acts as the messaging layer, providing reliable group communication, membership, and quorum functionality among the cluster nodes. It's the heartbeat of the cluster, ensuring that all nodes agree on the current state of the cluster and can detect node failures quickly and accurately. Without Corosync, Pacemaker wouldn't know which nodes are alive or dead.

Pacemaker, sitting atop Corosync, is the actual cluster resource manager. Its responsibility is to manage resources (like IP addresses, file systems, applications, or virtual machines) across the cluster nodes. When a node fails, Pacemaker detects this via Corosync and automatically migrates the affected resources to another healthy node in the cluster, ensuring service continuity. This automated failover is what makes Pacemaker so critical for HA. Resource agents are scripts that Pacemaker uses to start, stop, and monitor these resources. Red Hat provides a rich set of standard resource agents for common services like Apache, MariaDB, NFS, and many others, and it's also possible to write custom agents for proprietary applications.

Architects must also understand the fundamental HA configurations: active-passive and active-active. In an active-passive configuration, one node (the active node) runs the service, while another node (the passive node) stands by, ready to take over if the active node fails. This setup is simpler to implement and manage, as only one instance of the application is running at any given time, avoiding complex data synchronization issues. However, it means that the resources of the passive node are largely idle during normal operation. A common example is a two-node database cluster where only one database instance is writable at a time.

Conversely, an active-active configuration involves multiple nodes simultaneously running instances of the same service, distributing the workload across them. This approach offers better resource utilization and can provide higher scalability and performance. However, it introduces significant complexity, particularly concerning data consistency and state management across multiple active instances. For instance, a web server farm behind a load balancer is a classic active-active setup, where each server handles a portion of the incoming requests. Choosing between active-passive and active-active depends heavily on the application's requirements, its ability to scale horizontally, and the complexity an organization is willing to manage. For many critical services like databases, an active-passive setup managed by Pacemaker is often preferred due to its inherent data integrity advantages, while stateless services or those designed for horizontal scaling might benefit from active-active load balancing. Understanding these foundational concepts is crucial before diving into the practical implementation with Red Hat's HA tools.

screens.title: Introduction to High Availability (HA) and Red Hat's HA Stack
screens.subtitle: Why availability matters, and the building blocks Red Hat provides to keep services running.

narration.text: High availability is about keeping services running when people and businesses depend on them. In this lesson you will get a practical foundation: what HA means, two essential metrics that define recovery expectations, and the core Red Hat components that make clustering possible. We’ll connect the goals you set as an architect — how quickly you must recover and how much data you can tolerate losing — to specific tools and configurations that meet those goals. You will see why Corosync is called the cluster heartbeat and why Pacemaker is the resource orchestrator that moves services when failures happen. I’ll also preview active-passive and active-active approaches so you can begin thinking about tradeoffs in capacity, complexity, and data consistency. By the end, you’ll be able to name the primary HA building blocks, explain RTO and RPO in plain terms with an example, and state when an active-passive design is preferred. Keep an ear out for common misconceptions about idle standby nodes and about when multiple active nodes actually increase risk instead of reducing it.

keyIdea.title: HA reduces downtime and data loss
keyIdea.text: High availability combines design, monitoring, and automated failover so services remain available and recover within defined RTO and RPO targets.

narration.text: These objectives clarify what you will be able to do after completing this chapter. I will show how RTO answers the speed of recovery while RPO defines acceptable data loss, and we’ll practice with a business example. Second, you will explain why HA is critical in Red Hat enterprise environments and how it maps to operational responsibilities such as monitoring, testing, and capacity planning. screens.title: What is High Availability (HA)?
screens.subtitle: A clear definition, common goals, and a practical example

narration.text: High availability describes systems designed to operate continuously or to recover very quickly when problems occur. At its heart HA is about minimizing downtime for users and applications. Practically, that means two things: the system must be able to detect failures and it must be able to recover services or reroute traffic within acceptable time and data-loss bounds. A concrete example: an online store that cannot accept orders for thirty minutes may lose revenue, customer trust, and transactional integrity. If the business sets an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO of 15 minutes, the architect must design replication, failover mechanisms, and operational playbooks that meet those numbers. A common misconception is that HA eliminates all outages; it does not. HA reduces the frequency and impact of outages and provides automated recovery steps. Another misconception is equating redundancy with availability: simply adding hardware without detection, orchestration, and testing often leaves you unprotected. Key takeaway: HA is a discipline combining design, automation, and operations to meet measurable recovery goals. How would you translate a business SLA into a concrete replication interval and recovery test plan?

keyIdea.title: HA is purposeful redundancy
keyIdea.text: It combines detection, orchestration, and operational planning to meet business recovery targets.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › What is HA?
Definition
Systems designed to operate continuously or recover quickly to minimize downtime and data loss.
Example
An e-commerce site with RTO 30 minutes and RPO 15 minutes requires short replication intervals and tested failover so orders are preserved and service returns quickly.
Key Takeaway

HA is measurable: define RTO and RPO, then design to them with detection and automated recovery.

Common mistakes
  • Assuming more hardware alone guarantees availability without orchestration.
  • Setting RTO/RPO without testing recovery procedures.
  • Mixing active-active expectations with stateful systems that require consistency.
Try this
Take a business SLA and write the RTO and RPO. Propose one replication or backup change that reduces RPO for that SLA.

screens.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
screens.subtitle: Precise meanings, a business example, and architectural implications

narration.text: RTO and RPO are the backbone of any HA conversation. RTO defines how quickly a service must be restored after an interruption. RPO defines how much data loss is acceptable measured by time. Put simply, RTO answers ‘how fast’ and RPO answers ‘how much’. For a payments system that cannot lose more than 15 minutes of transactions, the RPO is 15 minutes. If the business also requires recovery within 30 minutes, the RTO is 30 minutes. Architecturally, RPO drives replication frequency, checkpointing, and backup cadence — for instance synchronous replication or frequent snapshots reduce RPO but increase latency or cost. RTO drives orchestration speed, automated failover, and runbook quality — faster RTOs require automated detection and migration. A common misconception is that low RPO and low RTO are free; in practice they trade off with complexity, cost, and performance. Another trap is testing failover only infrequently; without rehearsals an architecture may not meet targets under load. Closing question: given an RTO of 10 minutes, what operational automation would you prioritize to make it realistic? Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) means rto limits downtime; rpo limits data loss. design replication and failover to meet both, balancing cost and complexity.. In practical terms, precise meanings, a business example, and architectural implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RTO vs RPO
keyIdea.text: RTO limits downtime; RPO limits data loss. Design replication and failover to meet both, balancing cost and complexity.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › RTO & RPO
RTO — Recovery Time Objective
Maximum tolerable downtime. Drives automation and failover speed requirements.
RPO — Recovery Point Objective
Maximum tolerable data loss measured in time. Drives replication and backup design.
Practical example

If RPO is 15 minutes, replication intervals and checkpoints must keep data exposure below 15 minutes.

Implications
  • Low RPO often requires synchronous or near-synchronous replication and may increase latency.
  • Low RTO favors automated failover and validated runbooks; manual recovery rarely meets tight RTOs.
  • Both targets require regular testing under realistic load to validate assumptions.
Check your understanding
Given RTO 10 minutes and RPO 1 minute, which replication pattern and failover automation choices will you prioritize and why?

screens.title: Types of Failures and Their Impact
screens.subtitle: Hardware, software, network, and environmental failures and mitigation approaches

narration.text: Failures come in many forms and each has different operational implications. Hardware failures include disk crashes or power supply faults; they often require redundant hardware, automatic replacement policies, and replication to avoid data loss. Software failures — application bugs or kernel panics — can be mitigated with health checks, automatic restarts, and rolling upgrades. Network failures like router outages or cable cuts need redundant paths, link bonding, and heartbeat monitoring so cluster membership remains accurate. Environmental failures such as power outages and natural disasters require site-level redundancy and disaster recovery planning. A useful mental model is to ask: how quickly can the system detect the failure and how gracefully can service be moved or restored? An example: if a primary database server's disk fails, replication and a tested automated failover can move the writable service to a standby node with minimal interruption. A common misconception is to treat all failures equally: different failure classes need different strategies. Another pitfall is assuming software restarts are sufficient when the root cause is replication lag or data corruption. In short, identify failure modes early and map each to detection and remediation strategies.

keyIdea.title: Classify failures to choose mitigations
keyIdea.text: Hardware, software, network, and environmental failures each demand tailored detection and recovery strategies.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Failure Types
Hardware Failures
Disk or power failures; mitigate with redundancy, hot spares, and replication.
Software Failures
Application bugs and kernel issues; mitigate with monitoring, automated restarts, and tested upgrades.
Network Failures
Router outages and link loss; mitigate with redundant paths, bonding, and heartbeat checks.
Environmental Failures
Power outages or disasters; plan site redundancy and disaster recovery exercises.
Scenario
A router and switch failure can partition a cluster. Corosync membership detection and quorum rules dictate whether resources fail over; ensuring redundant networking avoids unnecessary split-brain events.
Misconception

Not all restarts fix problems originating in data corruption or replication lag; diagnose root causes, not just symptoms.

screens.title: Corosync: The Cluster Heartbeat
screens.subtitle: What Corosync provides and why membership and quorum matter

narration.text: Corosync provides the messaging layer that keeps cluster nodes in agreement about membership and state. It delivers reliable group communication so every node can detect who is alive, who is suspected of failing, and whether the cluster has quorum. Quorum is the simple rule that prevents split-brain: nodes must agree on a majority or a configured policy before making decisions that affect shared resources. For example, if a three-node cluster loses one node, the remaining two nodes still hold quorum and can continue to operate. If links partition the network and a majority cannot be established, Corosync's membership signals help prevent multiple nodes from simultaneously claiming the same resource. A common misconception is that Corosync performs resource failover; it does not. Corosync informs Pacemaker about the cluster state. Corosync is therefore critical for timely failure detection and consistent decision-making across nodes. A practical check: ensure your network topology supports low-latency, reliable messaging so Corosync can detect failures without false positives. What network redundancy and latency thresholds would you choose for a given RTO? Corosync: The Cluster Heartbeat means it provides reliable group communication and quorum so nodes agree on cluster state and detect failures accurately.. In practical terms, what corosync provides and why membership and quorum matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Corosync = membership and messaging
keyIdea.text: It provides reliable group communication and quorum so nodes agree on cluster state and detect failures accurately.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Corosync
Role of Corosync
Reliable group messaging, membership, and quorum services that let nodes agree on who is alive and whether the cluster can safely make decisions.
Why quorum matters
Quorum prevents split-brain by requiring a majority or a configured rule before resources are managed. Without quorum, unsafe concurrent actions can occur.
Operational tip
Place Corosync traffic on redundant low-latency links and monitor for message loss to prevent false failure detections.
Scenario
A three-node cluster loses one node. Corosync updates membership and the remaining nodes keep quorum and continue managing resources.
Misconception

Corosync does not move services. It informs Pacemaker, which performs the actual failover and recovery actions.

screens.title: Pacemaker: The Resource Manager
screens.subtitle: How Pacemaker uses cluster state to manage and fail over resources

narration.text: Pacemaker is the cluster resource manager that acts on the membership and messaging information it receives from Corosync. Its job is to monitor configured resources — IP addresses, file systems, applications, or virtual machines — and to ensure they run on appropriate nodes. When Corosync signals that a node has failed or left the cluster, Pacemaker evaluates policies and constraints, then starts, stops, or migrates resources to healthy nodes. Standard resource agents implement start, stop, and monitor actions for common services, and you can create custom agents for proprietary applications. A concrete example: when a node hosting a database becomes unreachable, Pacemaker uses a resource agent to attempt an orderly stop and then starts the database on the chosen standby node. A common misconception is that Pacemaker will magically heal data corruption; it manages service processes and resources, but correct recovery of state often requires application-aware agents and replication strategies. The key operational requirement is to configure agents and constraints carefully and to test failover paths so Pacemaker's automated decisions align with your business goals. Pacemaker: The Resource Manager means it monitors and controls services using resource agents and acts on corosync's cluster state to fail over or migrate resources.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pacemaker manages resources
keyIdea.text: It monitors and controls services using resource agents and acts on Corosync's cluster state to fail over or migrate resources.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Pacemaker
Role of Pacemaker
A resource manager that starts, stops, monitors, and migrates resources based on cluster state and configured policies.
Resource Agents
Scripts that implement start, stop, and monitor operations for services; the quality of agents affects failover correctness.
Operational example
Pacemaker migrates a database resource to a standby node when Corosync reports the primary as failed, using the database resource agent to start services cleanly.
Configuration notes
Define constraints, ordering, and location rules so Pacemaker places resources predictably during failover.
Misconception

Pacemaker does not repair corrupted data; it manages service lifecycle. Data integrity depends on replication and application-aware recovery.

screens.title: Resource Agents: The Actionable Scripts
screens.subtitle: What resource agents do and why they're critical for safe failover

narration.text: Resource agents are the small but essential scripts Pacemaker calls to manage a service's lifecycle. They implement standard actions such as start, stop, and monitor. Because resource agents encapsulate how an application should be started, checked, and cleanly stopped, their correctness directly affects failover safety and application integrity. For common services—web servers, databases, file systems—Red Hat provides standard agents. For proprietary or complex applications you must author agents that understand application state and recovery semantics. A concrete example: a database agent should verify that the database is consistent and ready to accept writes before declaring the resource started; otherwise clients may encounter corruption or incomplete transactions. A frequent misconception is that any script that starts a process is a sufficient agent. In reality, agents must include monitoring hooks, return appropriate exit codes, and be idempotent so retries behave predictably. Test your agents in a failover drill to ensure Pacemaker automation produces the intended outcome. Ask yourself: what checks must an agent perform to ensure safe promotion of a standby to primary? Resource Agents: The Actionable Scripts means well-designed resource agents enforce safe start/stop and accurate monitoring, making automated failover reliable.. In practical terms, what resource agents do and why they're critical for safe failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Agents are the bridge to applications
keyIdea.text: Well-designed resource agents enforce safe start/stop and accurate monitoring, making automated failover reliable.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Resource Agents
What an agent must do
  • Start the service cleanly and idempotently.
  • Stop the service safely, flushing state if necessary.
  • Monitor the service and return correct status codes.
Example
A database agent checks for replication health, ensures logs are consistent, and only then promotes a standby to writable.
Testing agents
Run simulated failovers and validate that the agent's stop/start/monitor actions preserve data integrity and meet RTO targets.
Common mistake

Using ad-hoc scripts without robust monitoring or idempotency leads to unreliable failovers and inconsistent states.

screens.title: Active-Passive HA
screens.subtitle: How primary/standby setups work, benefits, and when to use them

narration.text: Active-passive configurations run a single active instance while one or more passive nodes stand ready to take over if the active fails. This pattern is straightforward: the active node handles all work and the passive node(s) receive replicated state or stay synchronized enough to become active when needed. Benefits include simpler consistency models, less application-level coordination, and predictable failover behavior, which is why many stateful services like traditional databases choose active-passive. However, passive nodes often remain underutilized, which is a cost consideration. A concrete example: a two-node database cluster where only one node accepts writes; the standby receives replication and is promoted when the primary fails. Misconceptions include thinking passive means untested; passive nodes must be exercised to ensure they can become active cleanly. Another error is ignoring replication lag — a standby that is significantly behind will cause data loss beyond the agreed RPO. Closing question: how will you validate a standby's readiness before failover to meet an RPO requirement? Active-Passive HA means simpler consistency and predictable failover at the cost of idle resources; preferred for stateful services requiring strong integrity.. In practical terms, how primary/standby setups work, benefits, and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Active-passive favors consistency
keyIdea.text: Simpler consistency and predictable failover at the cost of idle resources; preferred for stateful services requiring strong integrity.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Active-Passive
How it works
One active node handles writes while one or more passives replicate state and await promotion.
Use case
Stateful databases where a single primary ensures data integrity and avoids split-write scenarios.
Risks & validation
  • Standby must be sufficiently up-to-date to meet RPOs.
  • Failover procedures must be tested to meet RTOs.
  • Idle resources increase cost; justify with business requirements.
Check this

Plan a failover test that verifies standby freshness, application start time, and end-to-end transaction integrity.

screens.title: Active-Active HA
screens.subtitle: Parallel instances, load distribution, and data consistency challenges

narration.text: Active-active topologies run multiple instances of the same service simultaneously, sharing the workload. This pattern improves resource utilization and can scale throughput, but it also introduces data consistency and state management complexity. Stateless services such as web servers fit active-active easily: each server handles requests independently behind a load balancer. Stateful services require careful design: either the application must manage distributed state safely, or shared storage and coordination mechanisms must ensure consistency. A concrete example is a web server farm behind a load balancer, where each node serves a subset of traffic and failures are absorbed by others. A common misconception is to assume active-active automatically gives better availability for stateful services; without proper synchronization or conflict resolution you may increase the risk of data inconsistencies. Another challenge is that failover is not simply a resource migration; it requires reconciling distributed state and verifying that continued operation meets RPO expectations. Closing reflection: for a given application, can you identify whether it’s truly stateless or whether active-active would require additional coordination to preserve correctness? Active-Active HA means better utilization and scalability for stateless services, but added complexity for stateful correctness and synchronization.. In practical terms, parallel instances, load distribution, and data consistency challenges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Active-active trades simplicity for utilization
keyIdea.text: Better utilization and scalability for stateless services, but added complexity for stateful correctness and synchronization.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Active-Active
How it works
Multiple nodes run the same service and share traffic, improving utilization and capacity.
Good fit
Stateless services or those designed for distributed state with conflict resolution.
Complexities
  • Data synchronization and consistency across active instances.
  • More complex testing and operational playbooks.
  • Potential for conflict or split-write scenarios without careful coordination.
Scenario

A web farm handling traffic behind a load balancer is active-active: adding nodes increases capacity and provides graceful degradation if one node fails.

screens.title: Designing HA: Tradeoffs and Decisions
screens.subtitle: Balancing RTO/RPO, cost, complexity, and performance

narration.text: Designing high availability is a process of tradeoffs. Start by capturing business objectives: RTO and RPO for each service. Next, categorize the service as stateful or stateless because that determines whether active-passive or active-active is realistic. Then choose your replication strategy and resource placement: synchronous replication tightens RPO but may increase latency, while asynchronous approaches reduce latency at the cost of potential data loss. Plan your detection and orchestration: Corosync must reliably report membership and Pacemaker must have correct agents and constraints to act. Don’t forget testing: validate failover under load, replay failure scenarios, and measure the actual recovery times and data loss. A common architectural mistake is optimizing only for cost, leaving RTO and RPO unmet in production. Another is not automating enough; manual steps rarely meet tight RTOs. Example practical step: create a checklist that maps each SLA to a replication mode, failover automation, and a quarterly failover rehearsal. Final reflective question: which single operational automation or test would most reduce your predicted RTO for a critical service? Designing HA: Tradeoffs and Decisions means translate slas into replication, orchestration, and testing plans; prioritize the smallest changes that most reduce rto and rpo risk.. In practical terms, balancing rto/rpo, cost, complexity, and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design is a sequence of choices
keyIdea.text: Translate SLAs into replication, orchestration, and testing plans; prioritize the smallest changes that most reduce RTO and RPO risk.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Designing HA
Design process
  1. Capture RTO and RPO from stakeholders.
  2. Classify the service: stateful or stateless.
  3. Select replication and consistency strategy to meet RPO.
  4. Define automation, agents, and constraints for Pacemaker.
  5. Test failover and rehearse runbooks regularly.
Example checklist item

For RPO 5 minutes: enable near-synchronous replication and verify replication lag under peak load during rehearsals.

Tradeoffs
Lower RPO/RTO increases complexity and cost; document tradeoffs clearly for stakeholders.
Misconception

Assuming that a tested failover in isolation proves readiness; you must test under production-like load and state.

screens.title: HA Terminology Matching Exercise
screens.subtitle: Practice mapping terms to Red Hat components and writing definitions

narration.text: A quick hands-on exercise helps cement terminology and component responsibilities. Create a simple text document and for each of these terms write a one- or two-sentence explanation in your own words: RTO, RPO, Node Membership, Resource Failover, Quorum, and Service Monitoring. Then, for each term, identify which Red Hat HA component primarily manages or uses that concept: Corosync or Pacemaker. For example, node membership and quorum are primarily Corosync concerns because they come from the messaging and membership layer. Resource failover and service monitoring are primarily Pacemaker responsibilities because it orchestrates start, stop, and monitor actions via resource agents. This exercise reinforces the separation of concerns and helps you remember where to look in a running cluster. A common trap during this exercise is to label everything as Pacemaker's responsibility; instead think about who detects the issue (Corosync) versus who acts on it (Pacemaker). After finishing, review your answers and perform a quick cluster map exercise to visualize which component owns each responsibility. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let’s consolidate the core ideas you should remember. First, high availability aims to reduce downtime and limit data loss. RTO defines acceptable downtime and RPO defines acceptable data loss, and both must guide design decisions. Second, Corosync is the messaging and membership layer that provides reliable group communication and quorum, allowing nodes to know who is alive. Third, Pacemaker is the resource manager that uses resource agents to start, stop, and monitor services, making automated failover possible. Keep in mind the practical tradeoffs: active-passive simplifies consistency at the cost of unused capacity, while active-active improves utilization but increases state management complexity. Finally, resource agents and regular failover rehearsals are operational necessities. If you can state these five points and map responsibilities between Corosync and Pacemaker, you have the essential foundation to begin designing HA for Red Hat environments.

keyIdea.title: Five essential takeaways
keyIdea.text: RTO/RPO guide design, Corosync detects and informs, Pacemaker acts, choose active-passive for consistency, and test your failovers.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Key Concepts
High Availability (HA)
Systems designed to operate continuously or recover quickly to minimize downtime and data loss.
RTO & RPO
RTO limits downtime; RPO limits acceptable data loss. Both drive replication and automation choices.
Corosync
Provides group communication, membership, and quorum services — the cluster heartbeat.
Pacemaker
Manages resources and orchestrates failover using resource agents.
Active-Passive vs Active-Active
Active-passive simplifies consistency; active-active improves utilization but increases complexity.
Resource Agents
Scripts that start, stop, and monitor services; their correctness is essential for safe failover.
Summary Takeaway

Design HA by mapping SLAs to replication, orchestration, and tests. Use Corosync for detection and Pacemaker for action.

screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: A brief recap to lock in three essential reminders. First, always translate business SLAs into RTO and RPO values, because those numbers determine replication and automation choices. Second, separate detection from action: Corosync detects membership and quorum while Pacemaker manages resource lifecycle via agents. Third, choose your HA configuration based on application statefulness: favor active-passive for strict data integrity and active-active for stateless scalability. Keep these three ideas in mind as you design or review HA architectures for Red Hat environments.
